content: 1. The financial instability faced by many women living with HIV must be recognized and addressed. This is particularly important when engaging these communities meaningfully, as their time and involvement are often uncompensated. 2. The guideline will be made available online for download and as a printed publication. Printed versions will be distributed to WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, national AIDS control partners, WHO collaborating centers, NGO partners, professional associations, and communities of people living with HIV. 3. Joint technical meetings with the WHO Departments of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and HIV will be conducted to share the recommendations and related products. These will include implementation tools for the new recommendations and statements of good practice. 4. For the recommendation on the safe disclosure of HIV status, WHO is developing a module for healthcare providers, particularly those offering HIV testing and counseling services. This module aims to assist women at risk of or experiencing intimate partner violence in making safe disclosure decisions. 5. The module will be used alongside the WHO clinical handbook, Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence, which provides comprehensive guidance for healthcare providers, including practical tips and job aids. 6. Two sets of evidence briefs will be created: one for policymakers and program managers, and another for healthcare professionals. These briefs will highlight the recommendations and address contextual issues related to implementation. 7. If funding permits, dissemination plans will include workshops and briefings with various stakeholders at global and regional levels. 8. Detailed plans for developing evidence briefs, implementation tools, and dissemination strategies will be formulated in collaboration with implementing partners, national stakeholders, and communities of women living with HIV. These plans will ensure that derived products are tailored to the needs of different national contexts. 9. The executive summary and recommendations from the publication will be translated into the six UN languages for dissemination through WHO regional offices and during meetings organized or attended by WHO staff. 10. The guideline will be launched on the RHR Department’s website and featured in HRP News, a monthly electronic newsletter with over 3,000 subscribers, including clinicians, program managers, policymakers, and health-service users worldwide. 11. The guideline will also be shared through knowledge-sharing platforms such as the Implementing Best Practices (IBP) initiative and the Interagency Working Group on SRH & HIV Linkages website. These platforms reach key partners working in the fields of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and HIV. 12. Several articles will be published to present the systematic and literature reviews conducted for the guideline's development. These will also highlight the recommendations and key implementation considerations. 13. A search function has been created by the RHR Department to allow users to search the database of WHO guidelines and recommendations. The recommendations of this guideline will be accessible through this new search function. 14. Effective implementation of the recommendations and good practice statements in this guideline may require reorganization of care and redistribution of healthcare resources, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. 15. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems must be practical, not overly complex, and capable of collecting current, useful, and applicable information. The implementation and impact of these recommendations will be monitored at health service, regional, and country levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators. 16. WHO and UN partner agencies have developed frameworks for monitoring healthcare and health system responses to HIV and SRHR in the general population and among people living with HIV. These frameworks include national-level indicators and actions, as well as recommended indicators at global, subnational, and community levels. 17. The Interagency Working Group on SRH & HIV Linkages and M&E experts have collaboratively identified and assessed existing indicators and tools. They have provided recommendations for a compendium of indicators to measure SRH and HIV integration and linkages at policy, systems, and service-delivery levels. 18. The SRHR and HIV Linkages Index has been developed to provide a composite score for measuring country progress in linking SRHR and HIV in 60 countries using 30 indicators. This index supports advocacy, guides decision-making for focused programming, and measures progress on SRHR and HIV linkages. 19. Data on countryand regional-level implementation of the recommendations will be collected to evaluate their shortto medium-term impact on national policies of individual WHO Member States. 20. The guideline will be updated five years after publication unless significant new evidence emerges that necessitates earlier revision. The WHO Steering Group will monitor research developments in SRHR for women living with HIV and address areas where evidence is lacking or of low quality. 21. Any concerns about the validity of a recommendation will be promptly communicated, and plans will be made to update the recommendation as needed. A scoping exercise will be conducted at the end of the five-year validity period to assess the currency of the recommendations and identify priority areas for new evidence-based guidance. 22. All technical products developed during the guideline's creation, including full reports of systematic reviews and search strategies, will be archived for future reference and use. 23. WHO aims to develop further guidance on topics that promote equity, are feasible to implement, and contribute to improvements in SRHR for women living with HIV. These recommendations will be included in future updates of the guideline.
